title: The return of the night train
text: The sleeper train was pronounced dead twice: once when cheap flights arrived, and once when budget airlines {{1}} the final blow. Both times the obituary was {{2}}. Europe's night network has {{3}} by a third since 2001 — and it is now growing again, with new sleeper routes {{4}} across the continent and state railways ordering sleeping cars for the first time in a generation. The reasons stack up. Flying shame is only the smallest of them: a bed on rails {{5}} a hotel night, city centre to city centre, no liquid limits, no airports at six in the morning. Business travellers {{6}} that a sleeper is a working evening plus a morning arrival; families {{7}} that children sleep through what would otherwise be a flight's most stressful hours. The old trains were {{8}} of a golden age that never quite was — cramped, occasionally late — but the refreshed carriages entering service now have proper showers, and the timetable keeps lengthening. The night train, it turns out, was never killed; it was merely waiting for the balance of cost and conscience to tip.

gaps.explanation: 'struck the final blow' — the collocation for delivering a blow; stricken is the adjective form, strive = try hard.
'the obituary was premature' — written before the death; pompous = self-important.
'has shrunk by a third' — the present perfect needs the participle 'shrunk'; 'shrank' is the past simple.
'new routes criss-crossing the continent' — crossing back and forth; digress = wander off the subject.
'a bed on rails replaces a hotel night' — substitutes for it; replenish = fill up again.
'business travellers note that…' — observe and record; notch = a cut marking a level.
'families report that children sleep through' — give as their experience; retort = reply sharply, recur = happen again.
'reminiscent of a golden age' — calling it to mind; remiss = negligent, reticent = unwilling to speak.
